title: MosaicMRI: A Diverse Dataset and Benchmark for Raw Musculoskeletal MRI
claim: The dataset spans many anatomies, orientations and contrasts, with a skewed but broad distribution, so it supports diverse training and evaluation.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right: donut chart of anatomy shares, 3x7 image grid
description: The left panel is a 3D-style donut chart of the anatomy distribution across 3,096 volumes. Slices are colored by anatomy: a large light-blue Spine slice (50.9%, 1,576 volumes), dark-blue Shoulder, light-green Hip, green Knee, pink Wrist/hand/thumb, red Ankle, orange and peach Foot, and small purple slices. White labels sit inside the larger slices, and percentages with volume counts sit outside on leader lines. The center reads '3,096 Volumes, 88,416 Slices, 854 Patients, 3 Orientations, 7 Contrasts'. The right panel is a grayscale MRI image grid. Columns are Spine, Shoulder, Hip, Knee, Wrist, Ankle and Pelvis. Rows are Axial, Sagittal and Coronal. The eye goes first to the big colorful donut, then to the grid of dark MRI slices.
caption: MosaicMRI overview. (left) Anatomy distribution for 3,096 fully sampled 1.5 T volumes, led by spine (50.9%, 1,576 volumes), shoulder (14.4%, 446), and hip (8.9%, 274), with all ten anatomy categories shown separately. (right) Representative slices spanning seven anatomy groups and three orientations.
abstract: Deep learning underpins a wide range of applications in MRI, including reconstruction, artifact removal, and segmentation. However, progress has been driven largely by public datasets focused on brain and knee imaging, shaping how models are trained and evaluated. As a result, careful studies of the reliability of these models across diverse anatomical settings remain limited. In this work, we introduce MosaicMRI, a large and diverse collection of fully sampled raw musculoskeletal (MSK) MR measurements designed for training and evaluating machine-learning--based methods. MosaicMRI is the largest open-source raw MSK MRI dataset to date, comprising 3,150 volumes and 89,830 slices, including a 3,096-volume 1.5~T core dataset and a 54-volume 0.55~T low-field set. The dataset offers substantial diversity in volume orientation (e.g., axial, sagittal), imaging contrasts (e.g., PD, T1, T2), anatomies (e.g., spine, knee, hip, ankle, and others), numbers of acquisition coils, and field strengths. Using accelerated reconstruction as a testbed, we study scaling, robustness, and data selection under realistic MSK distribution shifts. Across E2E-VarNet, U-Net, and ViT baselines, mixed-anatomy training improves over anatomy-specific training, showing that the benefit of anatomical diversity is not architecture-specific. Zero-shot experiments on the 0.55~T low-field set highlight that using more training data improves average reconstruction under field-strength shift. Controlled subset experiments further suggest that these gains come from transferable cross-anatomy structure, rather than anatomy or contrast matching alone.
